primaryQuery: how many smart home devices can a Wi-Fi router handle
readerQuestion: How can I tell whether my current Wi-Fi router can reliably support all my smart-home devices, and what should I change if it cannot?
selectedBecause: This question recurs from 2018 through 2026 across r/homeassistant, Home Assistant Community, current Google results, and a 2026 Home Assistant GitHub network-topology request. Searchers are shown conflicting universal device counts, theoretical association limits, address-pool explanations, and router marketing without a safe way to identify their own bottleneck. Current Cisco Meraki, Google, NETGEAR, Ubiquiti, and Home Assistant documentation supports a more useful model-first answer: the practical limit depends on the exact access point, traffic, airtime, signal, client distribution, address pool, backhaul, and router stability. Search Console contains no exact query, but it shows established Tara interest in adjacent network questions while every listed ownerPath remains protected. This capacity-assessment and upgrade-decision intent is broader than the other distinct finalist, durable across brands, a strong Tara fit, and not owned by Tara's mesh setup, VLAN, security-mode, static-address, or router-migration articles.

demandSignals.evidence: A homeowner whose lights, Alexa devices, and cameras exceeded an assumed 50-client ISP-gateway limit asks what can safely increase capacity, showing concrete pre-purchase intent rather than a single device symptom.

A later Home Assistant household still has about 50 Wi-Fi clients after moving many accessories to Zigbee and asks whether the router, DHCP handling, 2.4-GHz load, or access-point design is causing failed joins and random dropouts.

A prospective Home Assistant user plans more than 100 low-traffic accessories plus cameras and asks what number is realistically possible, prompting sharply different community numbers and underscoring the need for a model- and workload-based answer.

A homeowner wonders whether roughly 31 clients are overloading an ASUS router, while the thread reveals several alternative causes. This captures the recurring diagnostic problem: an offline entity does not prove that device count is the limit.

A June 2026 Home Assistant discussion requests a first-class IP-network topology view because access-point attachment, weak or wrong-node connections, and partial router-integration inventories are difficult to see during smart-home troubleshooting.

The exact-query review returns a thin Feit answer, a recent general guide, vendor client-limit pages, commercial router selectors, and pages that blur address counts with radio capacity. The result set answers with numbers more readily than it teaches a safe diagnosis.

searchReview.query: how many smart home devices can a Wi-Fi router handle
searchReview.intent: Find out whether the current router can reliably support a growing mix of plugs, bulbs, speakers, cameras, phones, and computers; recognize whether client count is actually causing dropouts or failed joins; and decide whether to change settings, add a wired access point, replace the router, or move suitable accessories to a hub-based protocol.
searchReview.resultGap: Current results commonly present one broad client number, a theoretical association ceiling, a product-family claim, or an address-pool explanation as if it were a dependable household limit. Even the stronger current guide is general rather than smart-home-specific. The results do not consistently explain that cameras and low-traffic sensors impose different loads; that association count, airtime, coverage, DHCP, processor stability, and backhaul are separate ceilings; that a VLAN or extra network name does not create radio capacity; or how to test the affected layer before spending money.

officialSources.name: Cisco Meraki maximum-client planning documentation
officialSources.supports: A theoretical association maximum is not a design target. Practical client capacity depends on the access-point model, Wi-Fi generation and client capability, coverage, backhaul, traffic type, interference, and airtime.

officialSources.name: Google Nest Wifi technical specifications
officialSources.supports: Nest Wifi Pro advertises up to 100 connected devices per router, but Google's footnote assumes no more than 1 Mbps per device plus sufficient broadband and coverage, illustrating why the conditions behind a product number matter.

officialSources.name: NETGEAR router client-limit documentation
officialSources.supports: Supported Wi-Fi client counts vary by router family, Wi-Fi generation, and number of bands rather than following one universal household number.

officialSources.name: Ubiquiti Wi-Fi connectivity and latency guidance
officialSources.supports: Current troubleshooting should inspect interference, airtime, RSSI, client band, access-point placement, and backhaul; adding access points without channel and placement planning can add interference.

officialSources.name: Home Assistant UniFi Network integration
officialSources.supports: The official local-push integration can expose WLAN client counts, per-client bandwidth, uptime, access-point state, CPU, and memory for supported UniFi systems, giving owners a practical monitoring path.

officialSources.name: Home Assistant DHCP discovery documentation
officialSources.supports: Home Assistant's DHCP Browser lists devices discovered through DHCP, ARP and PTR lookups, and router-based trackers, but it is a discovery view rather than proof of access-point capacity.

officialSources.name: Home Assistant Shelly integration troubleshooting
officialSources.supports: Missing local updates can be a range or roaming problem; the official documentation recommends checking configuration, moving the device closer, or adding a well-placed access point rather than assuming client count is the cause.

officialSources.name: Home Assistant Zigbee Home Automation documentation
officialSources.supports: Zigbee devices form a separate low-power network through a coordinator, so its end devices are not individual Wi-Fi clients even when Home Assistant controls them.

officialSources.name: Home Assistant Thread documentation
officialSources.supports: Thread devices use their own low-power mesh and reach the local IP network through a Thread border router rather than each joining the Wi-Fi access point.

officialSources.name: Home Assistant Z-Wave documentation
officialSources.supports: Z-Wave devices communicate through a separate Z-Wave controller and therefore do not each occupy a Wi-Fi client slot.

officialSources.name: Home Assistant ASUSWRT client inventory issue
officialSources.supports: A documented ASUS AiMesh case showed 57 clients in the router but only 22 through the Home Assistant integration, so a Home Assistant device count may be incomplete and should be checked against the router or controller.

existingCoverage.decision: The mesh guide owns coverage, placement, backhaul, roaming, and 2.4-GHz onboarding; the static-address article owns reservations; the VLAN article owns segmentation and local discovery; the WPA article owns authentication compatibility; the router-change article owns migration; and /home-assistant-smart-home-kit/ owns the closest commercial controller-and-network planning intent. The new article will own capacity assessment and the upgrade decision: distinguish the exact model's association ceiling from practical household capacity, identify which of several independent limits is failing, and choose the least disruptive remedy. It will link to those owners for implementation depth and will not publish a router ranking, repeat setup instructions, or create a competing commercial page.
